vignette:
Yousef is a 48-year-old fashion designer who lives alone in a converted loft in downtown Los Angeles, a space he once filled with sketches, fabric swatches, and the hum of a sewing machine running late into the night. He came to therapy six months after a fire broke out in a garment factory where he was presenting a new collection to a small group of buyers and journalists. The event lasted less than ten minutes, but for Yousef, it has never ended. The fire started in a storage room adjacent to the showroom, triggered by faulty wiring. He remembers the smoke alarm, the shouting, the crush of bodies toward the exit. But what he remembers most vividly, and what returns to him without warning, is the taste of the air-acrid, chemical, metallic-and the way the heat pressed against his skin, a specific, suffocating warmth that felt like being wrapped in something alive. He can taste that air in his mouth now, sometimes when he is simply sitting at his desk, and the heat on his skin returns so sharply that he finds himself checking his own arms for burns.

The memory does not come as a story. It comes in pieces: the sound of a woman's heel snapping, the sight of a ceiling tile falling, the sudden nausea that rose in his throat as he pushed through a door. These fragments do not fit together. He cannot arrange them into a sequence that makes sense. And when a fragment arrives, it does not feel like a memory at all. It feels like the event is happening right now, again, and he is inside it, trapped. This is what frightens him most-not the memory itself, but the way it collapses time. He has come to believe that his mind is broken, that he cannot trust his own perception of the present because the past keeps breaking through.

In the weeks after the fire, Yousef noticed that he could no longer tolerate certain temperatures. A warm room, a hot cup of coffee, the sun through a car window-any of these could trigger the nausea and the intrusive taste. He began to avoid warm environments entirely, keeping his loft at a cool sixty degrees and drinking only cold water. He also found himself checking the locks on his door and windows repeatedly before bed, sometimes four or five times, and then again after he had already lain down. He knew it did not make sense-the fire had not come through a locked door-but the checking calmed something in his chest for a few seconds before the doubt returned.

To keep the memories at bay, Yousef threw himself into his work. He took on three new clients, worked fourteen-hour days, and filled every evening with meetings and fittings and social obligations. He told himself this was productivity, that he was bouncing back, but the busyness was frantic, hollow. At night, alone in his loft, the silence would press in and the fragments would return. He began to hurt himself physically to release the overwhelming feelings-small cuts on his inner thigh, where no one would see. He did this perhaps once a week, and it worked, briefly, as a way to stop the spiral. He was ashamed of it, but he was more afraid of what would happen if he did not.

In public, Yousef's vigilance had become automatic. He could not enter a restaurant or a store without scanning the room for exits, noting the nearest door, the path to the street, whether the windows opened. He did this without deciding to; it was simply what his eyes did. He had difficulty concentrating during conversations because part of his attention was always on the environment-checking for smoke, for heat, for the signs he had learned to fear. Clients noticed that he seemed distracted, that he sometimes did not hear their questions. One long-term client, a boutique owner he had worked with for years, told him gently that he seemed "not himself." Yousef laughed it off, but the comment stayed with him.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in his own studio. He was alone, pinning a hem on a silk dress, when a warm draft from the heating vent drifted across his neck. The nausea hit him instantly, and he tasted the factory air. He dropped the dress, stumbled to the bathroom, and vomited. He stood there, gripping the sink, and realized that he could not keep living this way-that the fire had not ended that day, and that something in him was still burning. He is terrified that therapy will mean having to talk about the event in detail, to piece together the fragments he has tried so hard to avoid. But he is also tired, and he wants to feel like the present is real again, and that a warm room is just a warm room.
